overview: Maan here is not the Punjabi entertainer in the imported summary. The exact atlas record most plausibly points to Ma-in, the Minaean kingdom and trading communities of ancient South Arabia. Its heartland lay around Qarnawu and Yathill in Yemen's Jawf. Inscriptions, temples, irrigated fields, pottery, walls, and settlements document kings, councils, merchants, farmers, families, and worshippers. Minaic texts also trace mobile communities through Arabian oases, Egypt, and Delos. Scholarship debates the royal sequence and final political date, so the atlas span from 200 to 1 BCE is retained only as map coverage. The map is especially misleading: its single polygon covers much of the western Hijaz but excludes Qarnawu, Yathill, Dadan, and other essential places. It is neither a border nor a merchant itinerary. Daily life depended on flood irrigation, food production, skilled building, caravan work, households, and writing on stone or small wooden sticks. No source reconstructs every home, school, illness, or toilet. At 1 BCE the layer disappears, but neither Minaean people nor writing demonstrably vanished then, so the ending is a cartographic transformation.

periods.title: 200 to 175 BCE: western merchants and Delos
periods.summary: Minaean merchants operated far beyond the Jawf. A Minaic altar on Delos belongs to the first half of the second century BCE, probably after the island became a free port in 167 BCE. The atlas begins at 200 as a mapping interval, not a securely recorded royal accession.

periods.title: 175 to 150 BCE: families along caravan routes
periods.summary: Inscriptions at Hima preserve names and movements along a major Arabian route, showing that trade involved travelers, households, and repeated stopping places rather than colored territory alone. More than 150 Minaean texts there expand the social record, although their dates and purposes vary and cannot narrate every year.

periods.title: 150 to 125 BCE: fortified Yathill
periods.summary: Yathill remained a commercial and religious center with massive walls, towers, one known western gate, and temples. Its four-hectare enclosure concentrated impressive buildings, but people also worked fields and camps outside it. The phase labels are approximate because architectural repairs and inscriptions do not align neatly with twenty-five-year blocks.

periods.title: 125 to 100 BCE: mixed communities at Dadan
periods.summary: Minaic records at Dadan show sustained contact with local society. One damaged legal text addresses children born to a Minaean woman and a Dadanite man, while dating formulas reveal shared administrative habits. These documents establish interaction and law, not one uniform marriage rule for all Minaean communities.

periods.title: 100 to 75 BCE: royal chronology remains debated
periods.summary: Reconstructing Ma-in's rulers depends on inscriptions, genealogy, writing style, and uncertain synchronisms. A modern study orders thirty-nine rulers across many centuries, but alternative chronologies remain possible. This card therefore avoids attaching an unverified king or decisive political event to the atlas change at 100 BCE.

periods.title: 75 to 50 BCE: institutions in inscriptions
periods.summary: Yathill's inscriptions illuminate temples, buildings, rulers, and civic groups while leaving many ordinary activities unstated. Political authority may have been changing, yet a thinning royal sequence is not proof that residents, irrigation, worship, or trade stopped. Archaeological and epigraphic dates must be compared rather than forced into one collapse year.

periods.title: 50 to 25 BCE: a city already changing
periods.summary: UNESCO records Yathill as already declining when Aelius Gallus's expedition occupied it in 25 BCE. That military episode affected a particular city and campaign; it does not prove that Rome conquered all Ma-in or ended every Minaean network. The atlas polygon, far to the northwest, cannot map the expedition's result.

periods.title: 25 to 1 BCE: atlas endpoint without a fixed fall
periods.summary: The royal sequence is difficult to anchor, and scholarship continues to debate when the kingdom ended. The atlas removes Maan at its 1 BCE boundary, but no securely matching event justifies calling that a fall. Minaic identity and writing continued into changed political settings, so the close is explicitly cartographic.

sections.title: Exact identity, chronology, and atlas geometry

items.text: The exact id is maan, indexed as an approximate Asian state from 200 to 1 BCE. Its imported summary is a biography of Punjabi artist Babbu Maan, an unrelated modern person. The corrected identity is ancient Ma-in and its Minaean communities, while the exact id remains unchanged for atlas compatibility.

All fifty border snapshots were audited. Maan appears exactly once in the 200 and 100 BCE files, with no duplicate feature, interval mismatch, or lifetime violation. Coverage reports two files and two intervals; the live card index, card directory, override registry, and staged-draft list contain no exact association.

Both target features decode to one identical thirty-one-position Polygon with one component and one ring. Its bounding box is approximately 37.20 to 43.80 degrees east and 17.52 to 26.25 degrees north. The century boundary changes properties, not shape, so it cannot document a historical frontier revision.

Mecca, Jeddah, Medina, and Yanbu fall inside the polygon. Qarnawu and Yathill, the kingdom's principal cities, fall outside, as do Dadan, Najran, Qaryat al-Faw, Petra, and Gaza. The drawing therefore cannot represent either Minaean territory or the full trade network it may be trying to suggest.

At 200 BCE the feature shares atlas arcs with the Nabataean kingdom, Saba, and Arabs; at 100 it shares arcs with Nabataea and Saba. It has no measured area overlap or representative-point ownership overlap. Shared topology records drawing construction, not treaties, toll gates, diplomatic alliances, or controlled caravan stages.

sections.title: Kings, councils, law, and political evidence

items.text: Minaic inscriptions preserve a long royal sequence, sometimes including co-rule, but dates depend on genealogies, writing styles, and a limited number of external synchronisms. A reconstruction lists thirty-nine rulers from the eighth to first centuries BCE. That learned sequence remains a hypothesis, not a day-by-day court chronicle.

Ma-in developed from a Jawf city-state and later joined with Yathill, producing regional hegemony and competition with Saba. Excavated walls and settlement phases complicate any single origin story. The political community changed across centuries, so the atlas's late two-century slice should not be mistaken for its whole history.

A long Qarnawu inscription names Alman, his five sons, his clan, the king, and Ma-in's high council while recording towers, connecting works, land, farming, offerings, dues, and first fruits. It offers unusually rich institutional evidence, yet one monumental account cannot describe every taxpayer, tenant, or civic office.

The central Minaic corpus contains about 1,300 inscriptions, including royal, dedicatory, building, legal, and private records. DASI links texts to objects, places, bibliography, editions, and translations. Large numbers improve comparison, but damaged stones, uneven excavation, formulaic wording, and uncertain dates still shape what historians can recover.

Digital epigraphy lets readers compare spellings, personal names, titles, objects, findspots, and translations instead of treating an isolated line as self-explanatory. It does not turn the surviving corpus into a complete archive. Routine orders, oral agreements, failed petitions, and records on perishable supports may be absent or undiscovered.

The inland route linked Shabwa and Timna with Qarnawu, Yathill, Najran, and northern markets. Caravans depended on animals, handlers, water, fodder, guards, brokers, warehouses, and negotiated access. Aromatics were important, but a route also moved people, information, containers, food, metalwork, textiles, and obligations between communities.

The marginal Minaic corpus gathers about seventy inscriptions from outside the homeland, including north Arabian oases, Egypt, and Delos. These texts document people and institutions at distant stations. They do not prove that Ma-in ruled every place where a merchant prayed, married, wrote, stored goods, or paid a local authority.

More than 150 Minaean graffiti and inscriptions at Hima reveal repeated caravan movement and family integration along a trans-Arabian corridor. Brief names can establish presence but rarely supply cargo totals or travel diaries. A scratched name says someone was there; it does not hand us that traveler's entire itinerary.

At Dadan, Minaic and Dadanitic inscriptions show neighboring groups sharing an oasis while maintaining distinguishable writing practices. A legal text about children of a mixed union makes family consequences visible. Cultural contact could involve cooperation, law, worship, language learning, and tension without requiring one population to replace the other.

On Delos, Hani and Zaydil of the clan Khabab dedicated an altar to Waddum and the gods of Ma-in. The text belongs to the first half of the second century BCE; later Greek additions identified the deity for other readers. It is direct evidence of worship within a commercial Mediterranean setting.

Qarnawu stood on a raised rectangular site with a carefully planned street connecting western and eastern gates, temples, walls, and irrigated land around it. Its monumental plan shows coordinated labor, not the layout of every home. Crucially, the atlas polygon excludes this capital entirely, exposing the map's geographic mismatch.

Yathill occupied about four hectares inside a semi-oval wall roughly 276 by 188 meters, strengthened by fifty-six projecting towers and entered through one known western gate. These memorable numbers describe preserved fortifications, not a population census. People also lived, camped, farmed, buried relatives, and worked beyond the enclosure.

Near Baraqish, interlaced irrigation channels served more than 1,350 hectares, and a Minaean dam with an outlet and main canal controlled seasonal floodwater. Such systems required surveying, clearing, repair, and agreements about flows. They supported fields and animals but cannot be assumed to have delivered equal household water access.

Excavation uncovered a massive hypostyle temple dedicated to Athtar dhu-Qabd beside the Nakrah sanctuary. Columns, stairs, inscriptions, pottery, and offerings preserve ritual architecture and skilled construction. They reveal investment by institutions and worshippers, while ordinary houses and temporary shelters remain less visible than carefully built sacred spaces.

Area C cut through deposits beyond the Minaean wall, recovering layered structures, hearths, refuse, plants, animals, objects, and trade evidence. This sequence reminds us that a famous caravan city was also an inhabited oasis. Its residents cooked, repaired, discarded, and adapted as watercourses and urban priorities changed.

sections.title: Farming, food, crafts, and working lives

items.text: Baraqish began where seasonal floodwater could be captured and managed. Farming remained essential even when caravan exchange became prominent. Fields, palms, animals, and stored harvests depended on variable water and coordinated labor. Calling it a trade station alone would hide the people who made food before any caravan could purchase it.

Area C preserves carbonized and uncarbonized plants as well as animal remains from Sabaean and Minaean layers. These materials help reconstruct crops, herding, fuel, meals, and changing ecology. They are samples filtered by burning, dumping, decay, and excavation, so they cannot supply one universal Minaean menu.

Minaean pottery at Baraqish is classified by fabric, form, surface treatment, context, and sequence. Vessels served storage, preparation, serving, transport, and ritual. Regional styles can help date deposits, but a sherd cannot identify its user's language, legal status, gender, or political loyalty without supporting context.

The Area C catalogue deliberately includes humble objects because tools, fragments, production waste, and repaired things can illuminate behavior that prestige finds miss. Skilled work involved stone, mudbrick, wood, metal, fibers, leather, pottery, and animal equipment. Many crafts survive archaeologically only through durable scraps or indirect traces.

Caravan infrastructure joined wells, irrigated settlements, walls, temples, markets, roads, and stopping places. Maintaining it required local farmers and builders as much as long-distance merchants. The achievement was a chain of negotiated services rather than one endless camel parade moving through empty desert with no cooks, accountants, or repairs.

sections.title: Families, women, status, and social life

items.text: Alman's building inscription identifies him as a son, father of five named sons, clan member, royal favorite, landholder, builder, and worshipper. Those overlapping roles show family embedded in politics, farming, and ritual. They do not establish one household size or prove that only men contributed to the recorded projects.

Minaean records include marriages with women from other Arabian and Mediterranean communities. Such lists reveal mobile households, alliances, and legal recognition across distance. They preserve selected unions involving merchants and institutions, not a demographic survey, and they cannot tell us whether every spouse traveled willingly or experienced marriage alike.

The damaged Dadan legal inscription addresses the status of children born to a Minaean woman and a Dadanite man. It proves that mixed families raised questions requiring public rules. Because much of the text is lost, historians should not reconstruct exact custody, inheritance, citizenship, or affection from the surviving clauses.

South Arabian inscriptions show women as wives, mothers, daughters, dedicators, property holders, and partners in cross-community marriages. A bilingual dedication by a Minaean woman and Sabaean husband demonstrates negotiated identity. Elite or inscribed cases widen the record, but they do not represent every woman's work, freedom, or resources.

Pit graves west of Baraqish contained modest burials and inscribed stelae linked by excavators to seasonal visitors, perhaps a mobile community outside the walls. The interpretation connects town and caravan populations without making them identical. Grave simplicity may reflect custom, means, mobility, disturbance, or selection rather than lack of care.

No excavated building is securely identified as a Ma-in school for all children. Across ancient South Arabia, however, wooden writing exercises show a developed scribal curriculum. The evidence supports trained writers and teaching environments, while leaving attendance, age, gender, fees, discipline, and access in Minaean towns largely unknown.

Children also learned outside scribal settings by watching and helping with herding, food preparation, water management, building, pottery, textiles, trade, and ritual. Archaeological objects demonstrate skilled sequences but rarely name teacher or pupil. Household learning is plausible and necessary, yet exact ages and gendered assignments remain unrecorded.

Ancient South Arabian evidence suggests different levels of literacy: spontaneous names and graffiti, and more specialized written communication associated with temples and authorities. Monumental carving required planning and trained execution. Literacy was neither absent nor automatically universal, and knowing a name form did not make every writer a royal scribe.

Incised sticks carried letters, business accounts, money and goods transfers, debt settlements, contracts, requests, and ritual responses. They show that writing entered practical life beyond monuments. Minaic appears among these texts, although the largest surviving archive comes from Nashshan and cannot be assigned wholesale to Qarnawu households.

School exercises were found beside canceled deeds and correspondence, suggesting that archives could preserve models for learners. The Bavarian collection likewise includes legal texts and lessons. A palm-leaf stalk could be a contract, practice sheet, or letter, so calling every little stick ancient kindling would make a poor catalog.

The large Minaic corpus names people, dedications, works, transactions, and gods, but the reviewed evidence does not establish a standardized Minaean medical profession, hospital, pharmacopoeia, or diagnostic manual. That absence is limited to surviving and consulted sources. It does not mean households lacked remedies, nursing, specialists, or practical health knowledge.

Irrigation dams and channels supported food, animals, and reliable settlement, all of which affected health. The same standing water, silt, floods, and maintenance failures could also create burdens. Archaeology documents hydraulic capacity more securely than water purity, infection rates, equal distribution, or the daily labor of carrying household supplies.

Plant and animal remains can identify parts of diet and economy, but they do not by themselves diagnose nutrition, disease, or life expectancy. Burned seeds and butchered bones show consumption and disposal. Individual health would require securely dated human remains and context, which are much thinner for this exact Minaean interval.

The first excavated Minaean graves at Baraqish illuminate funerary practice and population movement more clearly than illness. Published summaries emphasize grave form, stelae, names, and visitors rather than a population-wide paleopathology. No rate of injury, childbirth risk, disability, or epidemic should be invented from those burials.

Temples, dedications, and divine requests show that people sought protection and addressed uncertainty through ritual. Digital editions can preserve the wording when texts survive, but they do not make every sanctuary a clinic. A prayer for well-being, a household remedy, and a trained treatment are related possibilities, not interchangeable evidence.

Baraqish's dam and channels managed floodwater for irrigated fields; they are not evidence of a sewer. No consulted source securely identifies a standardized Minaean toilet, household latrine, piped drinking network, or municipal waste service. Water control was sophisticated, but modern sanitation labels would claim functions the archaeology has not demonstrated.

Area C preserves hearths, domestic refuse, organic material, mudbrick structures, and deposits outside the wall. Waste was moved and accumulated in particular places, then altered by erosion, animals, decay, and later occupation. An excavated dump can reveal disposal habits without proving how clean every courtyard, street, or water vessel was.

Minaic used the Old South Arabian consonantal alphabet in monumental and minuscule forms. Public stone texts favored regular geometric letters; private wooden documents developed a quicker cursive hand. Script choice reflected surface and purpose, but neither form records vowels completely or guarantees that every speaker could read it.

Written-language sample, first half of the second century BCE, Minaic in right-to-left Musnad: `𐩢𐩬𐩱𐩽𐩥𐩸𐩺𐩵𐩱𐩡𐩽𐩹𐩺𐩽𐩭𐩹𐩨 | 𐩬𐩮𐩨𐩽𐩣𐩹𐩨𐩢𐩽𐩥𐩵𐩣𐩽𐩥𐩱𐩡𐩱𐩡𐩩 | 𐩣𐩲𐩬𐩽𐩨𐩵𐩡𐩻`. Transliteration: `ḤNʾ / w-ZYDʾL / ḏy / ḪḎB | nṣb / mḏbḥ / WDM / w-ʾlʾlt | MʿN / b-DLṮ`. Translation: “Hani and Zaydil of clan Khabab set up the altar of Waddum and the gods of Ma-in in Delos.” The Musnad is normalized Unicode rather than a facsimile; the dedicators are known, but the stone carver is not.

At Yathill, temples of Nakrah and Athtar dhu-Qabd preserve distinct divine names, architecture, offerings, and inscriptions. Religious practice involved communities and specialists but was not necessarily identical in every oasis or household. A temple's patron deity should not be expanded into a complete, fixed Minaean theology without supporting texts.

Minaean communities coordinated irrigated farming, walled cities, temples, caravan services, legal texts, household records, and long-distance relationships from Yemen to northern Arabia and the Mediterranean. Their achievement was sustained organization across environments and jurisdictions. It did not require direct territorial rule over every market reached by Minaic speakers.

Excavations at Baraqish recovered temples, walls, pottery, objects, graves, inscriptions, and deep settlement sequences. Modern conflict severely damaged the Nakrah temple and other remains, making archives and publication essential. Archaeological achievement belongs to ancient builders; preservation also depends on present researchers, conservators, Yemeni institutions, and local communities.

Roughly 1,300 central inscriptions plus marginal corpora and wooden documents make Ma-in unusually visible through its own language. The record includes kings and gods, but also families, contracts, buildings, farms, merchants, and learners. Its scale is impressive while still representing only what survived, was found, and has been read.

Minaic writing and Minaean identity did not necessarily end when royal power changed. A later wooden text may postdate the kingdom and names the God of Ma-in, demonstrating why state, people, language, and worship need separate timelines. Political disappearance is not a switch that instantly erases memory or community.

The atlas removes Maan at 1 BCE and leaves it absent at 100 CE. That display change supplies no safe successor: Saba, Qataban, Hadramawt, and Nabataea already have overlapping atlas lives, while the polygon omits the Minaean heartland. Transformation with no linked successor preserves the exact endpoint without inventing annexation.

ending.text: The card closes at 1 BCE because the atlas removes the exact maan feature, not because a securely dated conquest or social disappearance occurred then. Scholarship continues to debate the kingdom's final political chronology, and a later Minaic wooden text may come from after royal Ma-in. People, families, writing, trade habits, worship, farming, and place-based identities could persist under different authorities. No direct successor is added. Neighboring Saba, Qataban, Hadramawt, and Nabataea already overlap the mapped span, and the atlas polygon excludes Qarnawu and Yathill while covering distant Hijaz places. Linking any one neighbor at this endpoint would convert a coarse repaint into an unsupported transfer. Transformation with an empty successor list therefore records the map's behavior, preserves uncertainty about political change, and keeps social and linguistic continuity visible.
